items.title: Gemini 4 Argon (Fully Tested & Thoughts): It's Just Fake? I Tested It on 6 Hard Apps
items.summary:
In this video, I'll look at Google's new Gemini 4 Argon, starting with its pricing and the launch benchmarks, and why some of those charts aren't apples to apples. Then I'll go through what independent testers like Artificial Analysis, Vals, Zapier and Surge actually measured, where Argon leads on office work but is mixed on coding. After that, I run it on my KingBench 4 tests through Devin: an emulator, a Docker alternative, a 3D room designer, a QMK keyboard app, Pokémon Red and a Fitbit desktop app. Finally, I show the pattern I noticed, where it fakes the hidden parts of an app, and give my verdict on whether most people should use it.

--

💸 Gemini 4 Argon launches at $2 / $10 per million input / output tokens, and the price doubles to $4 / $20 after November.
📊 Google's launch charts have fine print, like a best-of-three-runs computer-use score and six times more checker time on a science test.

Now, back to the video. So Google has finally launched Gemini 4 Argon and I tested it on six really hard apps. The result is kind of weird. It built the best emulator and the best Pokémon game that any model has made on my benchmark, but it also built the worst keyboard app out of every model that I have tested. So is Argon actually better than Opus 5.5 and GPT 6.1 Soul or is it just better on Google's charts? Let's find out. Google teased and edged Argon for weeks before this launch. When they first teased it, I believe Opus 5.5 and GPT 6.1 Soul were not out yet, so Google might once again be late to the show. The model might have been a bit outdated before the general release itself or maybe they improved it in that time. We will see. Google says that Gemini 4 Argon delivers frontier performance in complex workflows. That means real software engineering, enterprise work like legal and finance and cybersecurity defense. Now, let's talk about the price. Argon launches at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Cached input tokens get 95% off the input price. After the offer ends, the regular price goes to $4 and $20, so it doubles. The intro price runs until the end of November, but to be honest, by the time it ends, we might see a new model anyway, so yeah. Google also says that it can now write up to 1 million output tokens in one go. The old limit was about 64,000. In simple words, it can think and write for a much longer time before it stops. That does not mean that every answer is better. It just means that it has more room. Now, in most of the benchmarks that Google shows, Argon beats Opus 5.5 except in a few of them. It also beats GPT-6, Astra, and GPT-6.1 Soul in most of But most of these benchmarks can be benchmarked easily. Benchmarking means a company trains or tunes the model to look good on the test and not on your real work. So, a chart is not always a correct way to check what a model can do. And if you read Google's own fine print, there are some fun details. On one computer use test, they ran it three times and showed the best run, and they only used part of the test. On a science test, they gave the checkers six times more time than normal. On a video test, Gemini got to look at more frames of the video than the other models did. None of this is cheating, but it means the numbers are not apples to apples. So, take the launch charts with a grain of salt. So, let's look at what other people measured. This is more useful. On Artificial Analysis, Argon scores 53 on their intelligence index. That is the same score as GPT-6, Astra on Max, and one point above GPT-6.1 Soul. Opus 5.5 on Max scores 58. Sonnet 5.5 scores 56. So, Argon is up there with the top models, but Anthropic is still ahead on this one. Now, there is one result here that I really like. Artificial Analysis asks models a lot of hard knowledge questions. When Argon does not know an answer, it usually says that it does not know. It makes stuff up only 15% of the time in those cases. Astra makes stuff up 51% of the time, and Soul 54%. So, Argon lies much less when it is unsure. But here is the catch. Argon also gets fewer answers fully right. It gets about 50% right, and Astra gets about 63%. So, it is more honest, but it does not know more. Those are two different things. The Valves Index is Argon's best result. It is number one there with 68.9% Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 are at about 67%. Zapier's Automation Bench is another good one for Argon. This test gives the model a business task across fake apps like a CRM and email. Then it checks if the work actually got done. The model saying done does not count. Argon gets 51%. And the next best, Sonnet 5.5, gets about 45%. So, it leads. But it still fails about half of the tasks. So, you still need to check its work. On Serge's spreadsheet test, Argon scores 38%. versus 30% for Opus and 23% for Astra. So, it is clearly good at reading and fixing Excel files. But on Serge's other test, which gives the model short and vague job requests in healthcare, Argon gets about 10%. Opus gets about 25%. So, when the task is unclear and the model has to figure out what you actually want, Opus is still much better. On EleutherAI, where real people vote on which answer they like more, Argon is number one right now. That is a good sign for chat. But votes are not the same as getting work done. Now, coding. This is where things get mixed. On Valves' app building test, Argon scores about 92%. Sonnet 5.5 is basically the same. Opus and Astra are around 90%. So, it is a tie. But the cost is not a tie. Argon costs about $8 per app. Opus costs about $58 and Astra about $39. That is a huge difference. On Terminal Bench 4, which tests agents working in a terminal, Argon is fifth on Valves with about 58%. Opus and Sonnet are around 64% to 65. On the science terminal test, Google reports about 58%. When Valves ran it, Argon got about 44%. behind Astra and Opus. The setups are different, so I can't say who is right. But it is a big gap. On code migration, which means moving code from one language to another, Argon is good at Java and weaker at Rust. Valse also rates how clean the code looks. Argon gets 3.6 out of five, Opus gets 4.5 and Astra 4.5. So, the code works about as often, but it is messier to read and maintain. One more thing on cost. Argon uses a lot of tokens. On artificial analysis, it writes about 62,000 output tokens per task. Astra writes about 27,000. So, Argon is cheap because the price per token is low. Not because it uses fewer tokens. When the price doubles after November, it becomes more expensive than Astra on Max. Now, that is the API side. Let's talk about if you want to use it where you can get it for cheaper like with a subscription. Well, technically you can find it at many places, but the plan from Google that gives you access costs $200, which is a lot to be very honest. I am a Devin ambassador, so I have access to the Devin Max plan and I used that to test it. The one place where I could use it was Devin. Devin has Argon in low, medium, and high. So, that is how I tested it. So, I have used it for the last 24 hours and I ran it on my King Bench four tests. These are six big apps from one prompt each. I used Argon on high through the Devin CLI. Each app was then checked in detail. That means building it, clicking through it, trying broken files, and reading the code. Let me go through them one by one. The first one is a Game Boy DS and 3DS emulator in Rust written from scratch. This is a crazy hard task. No model has done well here. Argon scored 5.2 out of 10. That is the best score on this task out of every model I have tested. Opus 5.5 got 3.7 and Solon Astra got 2.2. The Game Boy part actually works. It ran a home brew city builder game called U City and I could go into the city and open the build menu. Save states also work. But, the DS and 3DS parts are mostly for show. On the DS, a test program paints the screen red, but the screen stays black. The memory gets the red pixels. But the display reads from the wrong place. On the 3DS, it loads normal homebrew files wrong, so they just stay blank. And there is a small funny bug. The 0.5x speed button runs the game at normal speed, so it does not run most games like I asked. But it is still the best attempt so far. The second one is a Docker alternative. Argon scored three out of 10. It can pull images and manage them, and a lot of the local commands work. But there is a serious safety bug. When it unpacks an image, a bad image can write files outside of its own folder onto the rest of your computer. For a container tool, that is a big no. It also saves your CPU limit setting, but never applies it. And when it fails to download a base image, it quietly swaps in a fake one and does not tell you. Soul got five here, and Opus got 4.6. So, Argon is at the bottom with some of the smaller models. The third one is a 3D room designer. Argon scored 8.1, and to be honest, this looks really good. Let me show you. You get a warm lounge with a wood slat wall, a green sofa, lamps, a TV unit, and a bookshelf. The materials have that velvet and wood look. You can set the room size, create your own shapes like tables and arches, and change the light colors. And the light actually changes the color of the room. Export and import also work perfectly. But there are problems. If you look at the top bar, some buttons sit on top of each other. Auto cutaway and sunbeams cover the grid button. On a smaller laptop screen, buttons go off the edge. Undo after a size change jumps back too far. A broken scene file crashes the whole app, and it has a memory leak. Each time it redraws the room, it keeps the old 3D objects in memory. In the test, the same nine-item room went from about 100 objects to over 7,000. So, it is pretty, but it would slow down over time. Opus got 8.5, and Astra got 8.3. So, Argon is in the middle here. The fourth one is a VA alternative for QMK keyboards with a yellow theme. Argon scored That is the lowest score on this task out of every model that I have tested. Opus got 7.5. And this is the strange one because it looks great. The yellow and black theme is clean. It has key maps, layers, macros, tap dance, RGB, and a key list. But it never actually talks to your keyboard. You press connect, it opens the device, and then it throws the connection away. Every change you make only changes the screen and a fake log. So, nothing is ever saved to the keyboard. And the readme says that it has a real protocol engine and a flash button. That is not true on mobile. The left side of the keyboard is cut off. And if you import a bad macro file, the app goes blank. So, it is a nice mock-up, not a working tool. The fifth one is Pokémon Red in HTML from Pallet Town to the Rock Gym. Argon scored 8.7. That is the best score on this task out of every model I have tested. Astra got 8.5, Soul got 8.2, and Opus only got three. This one is actually playable from start to end. You leave your house, get your starter from Oak, fight your rival, get Oak's parcel from the mart, go through Viridian Forest, and beat Brock. You earn XP the normal way. Squirtle learns bubble, and you win the Boulder Badge and the TM. If you lose to Brock, you black out and lose half your money like the real game, and saves load back exactly. But the art is very basic. Look at Onix here. It is just a few gray squares. Oak's lab is mostly flat blocks. The routes are much smaller than the original. Brock's dialogue cuts off after three lines. And if saving fails, it still says game saved. Also, I noticed that it left a quest quick jump panel in the sidebar, which is labeled for testing. So, you can kind of skip right to Brock. Still, this is the best Pokémon run on my bench. The sixth one is a Fitbit desktop app with a Rust back end like the Whoop app. Argon scored 5.2. Opus got 7.4. Astra got and Soul got 6.6. Again, it looks really polished. You get recovery, strain, sleep scores, heart rate zones, and a health monitor. It looks like a real Whoop clone. The journal, the sleep planner, and the breathing exercises work. Data survives a restart, but the live sync with the Fitbit is fully fake. When you import a workout, missing heart rate values get filled in with made-up numbers. Sleep and recovery come from demo data, but the app shows them as if they came from your watch. And the health monitor says all your vitals are within range based on that demo data. If you change your max heart rate, the old numbers do not update. So, nice to look at, but I would not trust it with my health. So, the final total is 32.6 out of 60. That is about 54%. For comparison, Opus 5.5 is at about 58%. Astra is at about 57%. Soul is at 55%. And Haiku 5.5 is at about 54%. So, Argon lands in fourth place. It is basically tied with Haiku, which is a small model. One small note, Argon ran in Devon and the other models ran in their own tools. So, small gaps here are not a big deal. The cost was quite low. The six apps used about 772,000 output tokens. That came to about $10 at Devon's rates or about $20 at Google's intro price. And that does not include a few retries that I could not measure. So, the real number is a little higher. Now, here is the pattern that I noticed. Argon is really good at the parts you can see. The UI looks great. The games are playable and the main buttons work. But when the hard part is hidden, it fakes it and labels it as real. The keyboard app never talks to a keyboard. The Fitbit sync is fake. The Docker tool swaps in a fake image and it tells you that things worked when they did not. That is the opposite of what artificial analysis found in their questions. In chat, it admits when it does not know. In agent work, it pretends. That is a problem for anyone who wants to give it a task and walk away. So, let's conclude. Is Argon better or worse? It is better in some parts and worse in others. It is better at office work. That means spreadsheets, business workflows, and finance tasks. It is better at building games and good-looking front ends. It is better at saying, "I don't know." in chat. And right now, it is cheaper than Opus for a lot of these tasks. It is worse at vague tasks where it has to figure out what you want. It is worse at terminal and science work. Its code is messier. And in my apps, it fix the hard parts instead of telling you that they are missing. Overall, on my bench, Opus 5.5 is still better. Astro and Sol are also slightly ahead. So, should most people use it? First, most people can't even get it for regular use. You shouldn't pay like $200 for this model at all. There is no low-cost subscription that gives it to you today, except tools like Devin. Second, if you code every day, Opus 5.5 is still the better daily driver. And if you want cheap, Sol is still very cheap and very close. But if you have API access, it is worth a try for some things. Try it for spreadsheet work, for business automations, and for quick game or front-end prototypes while the intro price lasts. Just check what it says it did after November, when the price doubles. I don't think it is good value for most people. So, it is a good comeback for Google. It is a real frontier model now, but it is not the Opus killer that the charts make it look like. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like [music] this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking [music] the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music]

Standard Wonder finished this set at 45.8%. Its room designer and Pokémon game had useful working flows, while the systems and device integration tasks left major requirements unfinished. Full gives us a chance to see how much changes when we keep the requests and coding tool the same and select the other model. Muse Wonder is Meta's proprietary reasoning model family announced on October 12th. Wonder supports a context window of just over a million tokens, takes several kinds of input, and generates text. Through Muse Code, it can use tools to inspect a project, write files, run commands, and test its work. The weights aren't publicly available, so this isn't a model you download and run locally. Now, on the public benchmarks, Full has some stronger headline results. In the October 12th snapshot, Valves places it fifth on its index at 64.57% compared with Standard Wonder in 10th at 61.06. That index combines several professional task categories. It isn't a ranking of every possible use for an AI model. On Terminal Bench 4, Full is listed fifth at 58.08%. Fable has the same displayed score one place above it, so I'd keep that tie visible. On Vibe Code Bench, Full scores 86% and is listed 12th, while Standard Wonder scores 83.09% and is 18th. The improvement isn't across every row. On code migration, Full's point estimate is 61.03% and Standard Wonder's is 62.55. These individual benchmarks have uncertainty and their agents and tasks differ. They help set expectations without telling us how these six applications will turn out. Artificial Analysis gives Full 56 on its intelligence index compared with 52 for Standard Wonder. Its separate coding agents index gives Muse Code with Full 68 versus 63 with Standard Wonder. That second result measures the coding agent with the model. These published AA configurations use maximum effort, while our King Bench builds use high. Valves also lists maximum effort as its default with settings that can vary by benchmark. For pricing, I'm applying the same Standard Wonder rates to both runs. $4 per million fresh input tokens, $0.20 per million cached input tokens. Full's dollar figure is therefore an assumed API equivalent estimate. It isn't an official Full API price and it isn't an extra charge recorded on the subscription. >> All six builds were allowed to finish without an added generation deadline or model step budget. After each finished, I froze the files and tested a copy. The score comes from working requirements, correctness, presentation, and efficiency. with missing or unverified features reflected in the points. I didn't repair the apps before scoring them. So, let's open the results. The first project is the Game Boy DS and 3DS emulator. The request is deliberately broad. Build the systems in Rust, add the normal player features, and make most games work. Each console has to earn its own points. A good Game Boy implementation can't fill in the missing DS and 3DS functionality. Full produces a project called Tri Emu, and there is real work here. It has a Game Boy processor, graphics, and audio code, two arm processors for the DS, and an arm 11 path for the 3DS. These aren't just three buttons pointing to the same demonstration. The strongest part is Game Boy. I ran 29 public diagnostics, and 23 passed, including all 11 of the CPU instruction tests. An independent input test changes the rendered pixels. The audio code produces non-zero samples, and a battery save with actual data survives a file round trip. Restoring a valid state also resumes deterministically, but six diagnostics fail, and the independent checks expose timing and state problems. There's an interrupt sequence that leaves interrupts enabled when they should be disabled. Timer behavior is wrong. The first window scan line is offset, and restoring the real-time clock produces an incorrect result. A corrupt state can also be accepted and then crash when the emulator uses it. Those 23 diagnostic passes don't mean 23 games work. Diagnostics ask narrow questions about the hardware, and this run doesn't include a representative games library. So, the Game Boy result earns useful execution credit without earning the requested most games compatibility. On DS, both processors can execute a tiny independent test and write their own markers to memory. There is also a limited tile rendering path, but ordinary program counter relative arm instructions read the wrong location. Several interrupt and communication paths fail, and the standard frame buffer test comes out black. The 3D graphics and audio systems are missing. The 3DS side is even narrower. A small elf program reaches a frame buffer, but the standard homebrew format loading check fails. There is no working set of GPU, operating system, and audio services that would turn that into general 3DS compatibility. Then there's rewind. A single 3DS state is roughly 141 megabytes, and the default history retains up to 100 states. That projects to around 14.1 gigabytes just for those saved payloads. I didn't force the machine to run out of memory. The problem is visible from the measured state size and the actual history limit. Serializing one state also takes around a tenth of a second in this test. Full score is 3.1 out of 10 for the emulator, compared with 2.4 for standard Wonder. There is more working implementation, especially on Game Boy. The DS and 3DS requirements still account for most of the missing points. The second task is a Docker alternative. It has to accept Docker-compatible images, run containers, provide the surrounding life cycle and configuration features, and support the claim that it is more efficient. Full builds Light Box in Go. The interface covers much more than starting a process. There are image operations, build commands, configuration, and life cycle paths. The Linux source includes namespaces and resource controls, while the Mac development path is explicitly different. Compiling that Linux code doesn't establish that the isolation works, so I keep that part of the result qualified. >> The image handling has a more immediate failure. In an independent fixture, importing an image writes through a symbolic link and changes a marker outside Light Box's intended storage directory. Both the image and the marker belong to the evaluation, so no unrelated files are involved. The result demonstrates a real storage boundary failure. There's also a portability problem in its own export workflow. Light Box changes the layer archive when saving, but retains the old content hash in the image configuration. Loading the exported image then rejects the mismatched hash. A format-compatible file name isn't enough if the generated image fails its own integrity check and there is no comparable docker performance measurement, a small binary or a design with fewer processes can be interesting, but the requested efficiency advantage needs the same workload measured on both tools. The normal workflow checks find two more problems. Starting an existing container with attached output returns a success code even when its payload exits with an error. Running an extra command in a live container also replaces the saved main process identifier. That can leave later life cycle operations pointing at the wrong process. There are working features to credit. A real busy box image downloads and passes independent hash checks and the small native build environment, logging, and cleanup workflows run. The final result is 3.0 out of 10, the same score as standard wonder. The storage boundary failure caps it there. The third task is the 3D interior designer. This is where full gives us a much more usable application called atelier. You have a room in the middle, a furniture catalog on the left, and editing controls on the right. The dark interface has a consistent hierarchy and the scene contains recognizable furniture with shadows and procedural material. The basic editing is functional. Changing the room dimensions changes the actual geometry. I can create boxes, cylinders, spheres, and cones, give them specific dimensions and colors, and move them in the room. Dragging, rotating, raising, duplicating, and deleting objects all work in the targeted checks. The lighting controls also change real light sources with a visible effect on the scene. So, there's a useful starting point here. But, some everyday controls break the connection between what the interface promises and what the app does. Switch the units to feet and the label changes while the numeric entry still behaves as meters. Entering 10 gives you a 10-m room. Undo can leave the new room width or object color unchanged. The auto save problem is easy to demonstrate. Start with an 18-item scene, add one default box, and reload. You're back to 18 items. The app saves before adding the object. The earlier scene survives and this particular box can be restored with the same catalog click, but the advertised auto save has still missed the user's last action. Explicit export and import work, and editing the new box before reloading saves it in the follow-up check. Custom sunlight color also gets stored without being restored as the emitted color. Imported furniture accepts invalid sizes and duplicate identifiers, and imported labels are interpreted as HTML. Those are separate reliability problems, even though the normal scene round trip succeeds. The visual result has strengths, but the request was to make it look as realistic as possible. Here, the default bloom washes out the lighting, a huge bright sky plane is visible behind the room, and the floating dust looks more like snow. The furniture remains visibly assembled from rounded primitive shapes. It's a stylized room editor, and it doesn't earn all the realism points just because physically based materials are present. Repeated editing also leaves graphics resources behind. Five room edits take allocated textures from 53 to 83, while the scene still uses just 14 textures. After clearing 19 objects, the renderer still has 629 geometries allocated for only 28 active geometries. The source confirms missing cleanup. That matters in a design application where adding, changing, and removing objects is the normal workflow. Atelier scores 7.0 out of 10. Standard Wonder scored 7.6 on this task. Full has a substantial usable editor, but its editing and resource management defects bring this result below the standard model. The fourth task is a yellow-themed alternative to VA for configuring QMK keyboards. Full calls its app Hive Key. It has a clear keyboard editor, a searchable cue card palette, layers, macros, lighting, layout options, and a device panel. The yellow theme is consistent, and the selected key is easy to identify. Here, we need to look beyond the demo board. A keyboard editor can show a changed key while sending the wrong value to the device, so I check the messages against the actual QMK and VIA contracts. The browser tests use an independent firmware fixture. No physical keyboard was programmed, and the integration points reflect that limit. Full does implement discovery, connection, key map reading, and key map writing. Ordinary keys work in the fixture, and an imported custom keyboard layout sends changes to the correct matrix positions. Disconnecting and reconnecting also works. Those tests establish a working basic remapping flow within the fixture, but several of the advanced functions are wrong. Common layer switching keys generate incorrect numeric codes. Clockwise and counterclockwise encoder assignments are reversed. A macro that is supposed to press enter sends the written brace expression as ordinary text, because the action isn't encoded into the firmware's macro format. >> Lighting is another example of the interface claiming more than the device receives. The app sends the wrong addressing format. The fixture keeps its original brightness, and the UI still says the lighting was saved. A keyboard reporting four layers can also get a fifth layer added in the editor. The app claims a successful write, but reading back from the fixture removes that unsupported layer. Error recovery needs work, too. If a key write is rejected, the editor can keep showing the unsent key with no pending change indicator. Its exported VIA file doesn't match VIA save format, and reloading loses an imported board definition from the selector. Repeated connections accumulate input listeners, while returning to demo mode leaves the device open. Hive Key scores 5.5 out of 10, compared with standard Wonders 3.5. Full gets more of the connected workflow running, but I'd still need to fix those protocol and error handling problems before trusting it with a daily keyboard configuration. The fifth task is the opening of Pokémon Red from Pallet Town through Brock's gym. This is a good test of whether all the individual systems actually join together. You need the quests, navigation, encounters, combat, progression, and saving to support one continuous journey. Full delivers a browser game inside a Game Boy-style shell. The controls are clearly explained. There are on-screen buttons, and the page fits the tested phone width. It looks like a complete little game page when you open it. I started from the beginning and used normal controls. The Oak introduction, starter choice, and rival battle work. So do getting the parcel, returning for the Pokedex, buying supplies, catching a wild Pokémon, switching the party, and healing at the Pokémon Center. The path continues through Viridian Forest to Pewter City. Brock also has working win and loss outcomes. I first lost at level seven, which returned the party to the center, healed it, and reduced the money without awarding a badge. Then I trained through ordinary battles. Squirtle entered the final Brock attempt at level 10, reached 11 after Geodude, and 12 after Onix, and earned the Boulder Badge. Saving and selecting continue preserves the earned badge, party, money, and location. The model's own smoke test uses teleports and level changes, but this result comes from playing the route. That distinction gives us a much better picture of what a player can actually finish. The main weakness is fidelity. Oak's lab uses grassy ground and a row of outdoor trees with crate-like furniture. The gym has similar problems. Towns and roads are simplified into broad corridors, and the Pokémon are crude-drawn silhouettes. The browser shell has more polish than the world inside it. Some mechanics are simplified or incomplete as well. The northward quest gate is missing. The PC can store Pokémon without a corresponding withdrawal workflow, and the awarded move item acts as a souvenir. Those details matter for a recreation, even though they don't stop this particular route to Brock. The game scores 7.8 out of 10, up from Standard Wonders 7.2. It earns the full gym completion point because the route and both outcomes were demonstrated. The missing fidelity and secondary mechanics keep it from scoring as a faithful finished recreation. The last task is the Fitbit application. I asked for a desktop app with a Rust back-end, workout analytics, cardio load, and the kind of connected features you get in Hoop.
